title: The ruru deer
hookLine: a golden deer saves a drowning man, who later betrays him to the king
last: HAMSA — GREED PLUCKS THE GOOSE BARE.

cards: Money lent and quietly never mentioned again. A favor nobody returned. A door held open, and the person walks through looking at a phone.
A small voice says: next time, don't bother. Today's story is for that voice, and it's the last of the short stories: number 482 in the Jataka, the tales of the Buddha's earlier lives.
A deer with a coat like gold, a river in flood, and a man shouting for help. A short story about a long question: why do good for people who won't thank you?

teach.b: A young man from a rich family has wasted everything. Buried in debt, he throws himself into the Ganges. Then, in the water, he changes his mind and screams for help.
On the bank lives a ruru deer, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, with golden skin and a gentle voice. He wades into the current, lets the man grab hold, and carries him to shore.
He warms him, feeds him, shows him the road home, and asks one thing: don't tell anyone where I live. The man promises.
Meanwhile, in the city, the queen dreams of a golden deer teaching the law, and asks the king to find him. The king offers a reward: a village, and a thousand coins.
The man he saved hears it, goes straight to the palace, and leads the king to the river. The king raises his bow. The deer speaks, in a human voice, and asks who showed him the way.
Hearing the whole story, the king is so disgusted he wants to shoot the traitor instead. And here's the turn that makes it a Jataka. The deer steps between them and asks the king to spare the man.
The king lets him go, takes the deer to the city with honor, and the deer teaches the court.

teach.h: THE MAN SELLS HIM TO THE KING.
teach.b: The point isn't that people are awful, though the story is honest that some are.
It's where the deer's goodness lives.
It never depended on the man's gratitude. The ingratitude doesn't cancel the rescue. It just shows who each of them was.

how: Buddhists tell Jataka stories like this one in temples, schools and at home, and Buddhist teaching holds up doing good without expecting a return as part of the perfection of giving.

o: a cry for help from the river
a reward of a village and coins
a kind of deer named in old texts

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: carried the drowning man to shore
led the king to the river for a reward
dreamed of a golden deer teaching

s: the story ends with the deer taking revenge on the man
the deer asks the king to spare him: he saves the man a second time.
the man had promised not to tell where the deer lived
the deer asked one thing in return, and the man broke it for a reward.
the story says most people are ungrateful
it's honest that some are, but its point is that the deer's goodness never depended on thanks.

games.q: you're the golden deer. the man who betrayed you is about to be shot by the king. what do you do?
o: ask the king to spare him.
games.why: the deer steps in and asks for the man's life. the king spares him, and the deer goes on to teach the court.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing you did that nobody thanked you for, and notice whatever comes with it, maybe a sting, maybe a little scorekeeping.
Now picture the deer on the riverbank, choosing to wade in, and let your act stand on its own, finished and complete, whether or not anyone saw.
If a thought comes up about what they owe you, let it float past like a leaf on the river.

wordCard.voice: Ruru. The golden deer who saved a drowning man, was betrayed by him, and then saved him again.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: a kind of deer; the Ruru Jataka is number 482 in the Pali collection.

carryVoice: Your line: do it anyway. The deer saved him twice, and never asked for thanks. See you tomorrow.
